## Response

<!-- RESPONSE-START -->
I recently saw a headline along the lines of "Teens who use social media are more likely to be depressed." At face value, this statement claims that one thing, social media use, causes another, depression. However, based on what I learned in Chapter 10 of the course park, that claim is not necessarily valid. The chapter reminds us that to infer causality, three criteria must be met: temporal ordering (cause precedes effect), association (two variables must covary), and non-spuriousness (no alternate explanation or confounder). In the social media/depression example, we might find an association (teens who use more social media also report higher depression), so the associatuon criteria is satisfied. But we don't automatically know that social media use came before the depression, and we certainly don't know that some unmeasured third variable  isn't causing both. For example, maybe teens who are already lonely or in stressful home environments both turn to social media and become depressed, so the social media usage might simply be a symptom or coincident factor rather than the cause. The chapter uses a similar example with violent video games and aggression to illustrate that survey research alone cannot establish causality. To make the claim confidently that social media causes depression, the appropriate design would be a true experiment where you manipulate the independent variable and randomly assign participants to conditions, and then measure depression outcomes. According to the chapter, a true experiment builds in manipulation, random assignment, and control over the environment to satisfy those three criteria of causation.In short: the headline may reflect a correlation, but unless it comes from a design that ensures temporal precedence and rules out contradictions via random assignment and control, it is not justified in stating a causal relationship.
<!-- RESPONSE-END -->

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
